a.xlink:title: A production Nebari deployment with DSP must provide reliable RWX storage for group collaboration.
a.text: RWX is a core platform capability

a.xlink:title: The platform contract should describe observable behavior rather than mandate one storage product.
Providers without a suitable managed RWX service require an in-cluster implementation.
Mounting the home across a distributed Ray cluster requires RWX or an equivalent multi-node filesystem contract; single-node Ray does not.
a.text: Ray home access needs a portable

a.xlink:title: Dharhas Pothina proposed building a container from each user's Nebi or pixi definition before cluster launch, publishing it to Artifact Keeper or another configured registry, and having every autoscaled worker pull the same tagged image. This avoids rebuilding environments on each new worker and narrows the home mount to user files rather than environment trees. The integration and end-to-end workflow remain open design work.

environments on each new worker and
narrows the home mount to user files

a.xlink:title: RWX is unnecessary if every collaborating pod remains on one node.
Group co-location trades a storage requirement for an unsustainable compute constraint.
Kubernetes permits several pods on one node to mount the same RWO volume, so required affinity could force every collaborating pod onto one node.
a.text: one node to mount the same RWO

a.xlink:title: `/shared` can be replaced with buckets.
Use object storage for object-native data and mounted RWX storage where POSIX sharing is required.

a.xlink:title: Object storage supports concurrent multi-node access and is the preferred medium for large datasets and immutable artifacts.
Large datasets belong in object storage; homes, outputs, environments, and shared small-file workflows remain on volume storage.
a.text: Object storage is the default for

a.xlink:title: Nebari should standardize the RWX contract and acceptance criteria while allowing each infrastructure provider to supply the implementation.
The architecture may use any managed RWX provider that satisfies the performance, availability, operations, backup, and cost gates.
a.text: The architecture may use any managed

a.xlink:title: Shapes using managed RWX do not depend on FSx. EFS avoids a new integration, while FSx has a modeled recurring-cost advantage: $122-$1,127 per month at 50 users and $814-$4,834 per month at 200 users. FSx must recover its one-time integration and continuing maintenance cost across the expected cluster fleet and lifetime; EFS must not accumulate more recurring cost over that period than the integration work it avoids. The ranges remain uncertain because shared-storage I/O and EFS lifecycle tiering are not measured.

a.xlink:title: One Longhorn implementation across providers reduces differences in support and recovery procedures.
Longhorn can remain an RWX provider while native block storage serves single-pod workloads, provided each stateful workload has its own availability and durability design.
a.text: Longhorn can remain an RWX provider

a.xlink:title: The model assigns approximately 9.3 operator hours per Longhorn cluster per month and 2.3 hours to the managed-filesystem residual, a difference of about seven hours. The estimate comes from runbooks and observed incidents rather than time-tracking data.

a.xlink:title: A node-group disk resize encounters the instance-manager PDB while the node holds the final replica. Maintenance therefore requires replica movement or an explicit relaxation of the data-safety policy.

Longhorn reserves 25% of the node disk. After system use, NIC's 20 GiB default leaves roughly 2.4 GiB schedulable, so a 20 GiB Longhorn volume faults instead of provisioning. NIC can correct this through defaults or validation, but operators otherwise need to understand the hidden capacity rule.
a.text: Default AWS disks cannot hold the
disk. After system use, NIC's 20 GiB

a.xlink:title: Longhorn adds storage-specific procedures to normal cluster operations.
Replication is distributed, but access to the shared volume is not.
a.text: access to the shared volume is not.

Data-intensive jobs can copy inputs to node-local storage, execute there, and save results back to durable storage.

a.xlink:title: The Longhorn incumbent costs 2.5-2.7x the gp3-homes plus FSx Single-AZ shared-storage shape at each modeled tier.

The Multi-AZ FSx shape that places both homes and `/shared` on managed RWX costs $231, $1,083, and $6,307, effectively the same as the $231, $1,045, and $6,235 Longhorn incumbent while carrying the home-latency penalty.
a.text: Managed homes do not produce the
The Multi-AZ FSx shape that places

a.xlink:title: Longhorn's main cost is replicated capacity and supporting compute.
Every shape prices homes by requested capacity rather than actual use. Reducing oversized requests has 2.67x the effect under Longhorn and requires no backend migration.
a.text: Every shape prices homes by requested

a.xlink:title: EFS Elastic stays flat under measured concurrency but charges per GiB read and written. FSx uses provisioned throughput with a fixed bill and a purchasable ceiling. The model places EFS $122-$1,127 per month above FSx at 50 users and $814-$4,834 above it at 200 users, but actual shared-storage I/O and EFS lifecycle tiering are required to compare them confidently.

a.xlink:title: Longhorn is least compelling on providers that already supply the required capabilities as managed services.
Provider-native storage improves each runtime at the cost of separate driver, identity, ownership, capacity, failure, backup, and restore surfaces.
a.text: runtime at the cost of separate

a.xlink:title: Longhorn provides one storage vocabulary and recovery model while retaining provider-specific node, credential, backup, and infrastructure work.
Provider-native storage creates a distinct implementation and operating surface on each cloud.
GCP and Azure behavior is based on vendor documentation rather than Nebari deployment tests. Version, region, performance, and operational fit remain evaluation work.

a.xlink:title: EBS-backed workloads need guaranteed capacity in their volume's AZ, through per-AZ node groups, Karpenter, or a workload-level HA design with verified zone placement.

Keycloak currently runs one CNPG instance. Any shape that moves its volume to gp3 must either supply compute in that volume's AZ or add multiple CNPG instances with verified zone placement; database backup remains a separate requirement.

Removing Longhorn from RWO volumes exposes the fact that EBS remains bound to one AZ.

a.xlink:title: Per-AZ node groups duplicate scaling bounds, labels, taints, instance choices, and headroom. Karpenter avoids that fan-out but replaces Cluster Autoscaler.
Nebari has no stated availability objective for interactive user workloads, so the acceptability of waiting for an EBS volume's AZ cannot be derived from current requirements.

a.xlink:title: Nebi must tolerate loss and rematerialize the workspace before this PVC becomes ephemeral.

Holding the engine constant, Longhorn RWO to RWX costs 16-37x on untar, clone, and checkout. Against gp3, managed RWX costs 19-47x for FSx Single-AZ, 26-57x for FSx Multi-AZ, and 47-100x for EFS Elastic.

a.xlink:title: The managed design trades per-volume machinery for a broader managed-service dependency.

EFS access points and FSx child volumes expose different quota, resize, snapshot, and deletion behavior. For FSx, child volumes can be quota-limited or share a growable parent pool but cannot combine a hard quota with in-place growth; the filesystem grows by at least 10%, has a six-hour cooldown, and never shrinks. Each candidate needs its own StorageClass and lifecycle contract.
